Class ParticleFilter<States extends Num, Inputs extends Num, Outputs extends Num>

java.lang.Object
org.wpilib.math.estimator.ParticleFilter<States,Inputs,Outputs>
Type Parameters:
States - Number of states.
Inputs - Number of inputs.
Outputs - Number of outputs.
All Implemented Interfaces:
KalmanTypeFilter<States,Inputs,Outputs>
public class ParticleFilter<States extends Num, Inputs extends Num, Outputs extends Num> extends Object implements KalmanTypeFilter<States,Inputs,Outputs>
A particle filter estimates the state of a system by representing the state distribution with a set of weighted samples called particles. Unlike Kalman filters, it doesn't assume the state distribution is Gaussian, so it can handle strongly nonlinear models and multimodal distributions.

Each prediction step propagates every particle through the dynamics model and adds sampled process noise. Each correction step reweights the particles by the likelihood of the measurement given each particle, then resamples the particles if too few of them carry most of the weight.

The state estimate x-hat is the weighted mean of the particles, and the error covariance P is their weighted sample covariance.

The filter's computational cost is proportional to the number of particles. More particles give a more accurate approximation of the state distribution.

This class implements the generic particle filter in [2, Algorithm 3, p. 180] with the dynamics model as the importance density [2, eq. (62), p. 179]. That importance density comes from the bootstrap filter [1, Section 3.1, p. 108], also known as the sampling importance resampling (SIR) filter [2, Section V-B1, p. 181]. Unlike those filters, this one only resamples when the effective sample size is low instead of every timestep.

As shown in [2, eq. (49), p. 178], the N particles xᵢ with weights Wᵢ approximate the posterior state distribution as 

  p(xₖ | y₁, …, yₖ) ≈ Σᵢ Wᵢ δ(xₖ − xᵢ)

where δ is the Dirac delta and Σᵢ Wᵢ = 1.

References:

[1] N. J. Gordon, D. J. Salmond, and A. F. M. Smith, "Novel approach to nonlinear/non-Gaussian Bayesian state estimation," IEE Proceedings F, vol. 140, no. 2, pp. 107–113, 1993. DOI: 10.1049/ip-f-2.1993.0015 https://www.ece.iastate.edu/~namrata/EE520/Gordonnovelapproach.pdf

[2] M. S. Arulampalam, S. Maskell, N. Gordon, and T. Clapp, "A tutorial on particle filters for online nonlinear/non-Gaussian Bayesian tracking," IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing, vol. 50, no. 2, pp. 174–188, 2002. DOI: 10.1109/78.978374 https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~pabbeel/cs287-fa12/optreadings/Arulampalam_etal_2002.pdf

[3] R. Douc, O. Cappé, and E. Moulines, "Comparison of resampling schemes for particle filtering," Proceedings of the 4th International Symposium on Image and Signal Processing and Analysis (ISPA), pp. 64–69, 2005. https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0507025

  • Constructor Details

    • ParticleFilter

      public ParticleFilter(Nat<States> states, Nat<Outputs> outputs, BiFunction<Matrix<States,N1>, Matrix<Inputs,N1>, Matrix<States,N1>> f, BiFunction<Matrix<States,N1>, Matrix<Inputs,N1>, Matrix<Outputs,N1>> h, Matrix<States,N1> stateStdDevs, Matrix<Outputs,N1> measurementStdDevs, int numParticles, double dt)
      Constructs a particle filter.

      All particles start at the zero state, so the initial error covariance is zero. Call setXhat() and setP() to set the initial state distribution.

      See https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html#process-and-measurement-noise-covariance-matrices for how to select the standard deviations.

      Parameters:
      states - A Nat representing the number of states.
      outputs - A Nat representing the number of outputs.
      f - A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the derivative of the state vector.
      h - A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the measurement vector.
      stateStdDevs - Standard deviations of model states.
      measurementStdDevs - Standard deviations of measurements.
      numParticles - Number of particles. Must be positive.
      dt - Nominal discretization timestep in seconds.
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if numParticles isn't positive.

    • ParticleFilter

      public ParticleFilter(Nat<States> states, Nat<Outputs> outputs, BiFunction<Matrix<States,N1>, Matrix<Inputs,N1>, Matrix<States,N1>> f, BiFunction<Matrix<States,N1>, Matrix<Inputs,N1>, Matrix<Outputs,N1>> h, Matrix<States,N1> stateStdDevs, Matrix<Outputs,N1> measurementStdDevs, BiFunction<Matrix<States,?>, Matrix<?,N1>, Matrix<States,N1>> meanFuncX, BiFunction<Matrix<States,N1>, Matrix<States,N1>, Matrix<States,N1>> residualFuncX, BiFunction<Matrix<Outputs,N1>, Matrix<Outputs,N1>, Matrix<Outputs,N1>> residualFuncY, BiFunction<Matrix<States,N1>, Matrix<States,N1>, Matrix<States,N1>> addFuncX, int numParticles, double dt)
      Constructs a particle filter with custom mean, residual, and addition functions. Using custom functions for arithmetic can be useful if you have angles in the state or measurements, because they allow you to correctly account for the modular nature of angle arithmetic (see AngleStatistics.angleMean(), AngleStatistics.angleResidual(), and AngleStatistics.angleAdd()).

      All particles start at the zero state, so the initial error covariance is zero. Call setXhat() and setP() to set the initial state distribution.

      See https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/state-space/state-space-observers.html#process-and-measurement-noise-covariance-matrices for how to select the standard deviations.

      Parameters:
      states - A Nat representing the number of states.
      outputs - A Nat representing the number of outputs.
      f - A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the derivative of the state vector.
      h - A vector-valued function of x and u that returns the measurement vector.
      stateStdDevs - Standard deviations of model states.
      measurementStdDevs - Standard deviations of measurements.
      meanFuncX - A function that computes the weighted mean of the particles (one particle per column) given a column vector of weights that sum to one.
      residualFuncX - A function that computes the residual of two state vectors (i.e. it subtracts them.)
      residualFuncY - A function that computes the residual of two measurement vectors (i.e. it subtracts them.)
      addFuncX - A function that adds two state vectors.
      numParticles - Number of particles. Must be positive.
      dt - Nominal discretization timestep in seconds.
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if numParticles isn't positive.

    • correct

      public <Rows extends Num> void correct(Nat<Rows> rows, Matrix<Inputs,N1> u, Matrix<Rows,N1> y, BiFunction<Matrix<States,N1>, Matrix<Inputs,N1>, Matrix<Rows,N1>> h, Matrix<Rows,Rows> R)
      Correct the state estimate x-hat using the measurements in y.

      This is useful for when the measurements available during a timestep's correct() call vary. The h(x, u) passed to the constructor is used if one is not provided (the two-argument version of this function).
